Black River band (Ojibwe)

Black River is a historical band-name route connected to the Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe. The 1836 treaty names Swan Creek and Black River bands and lists a tract at the mouth of Black River of the St. Clair River. The 1855 treaty separately identifies the portions remaining in Michigan.

Read the sources [2] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties; historical treaty text [3] Clarke Historical Library, Central Michigan University; historical treaty text [1] Ziibiwing Center

Historical/constituent band-name reading route; related present government is the Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe. The three routes are not three newly established present nations.

  1. Treaty with the Chippewa, May 9, 1836 (7 Stat. 503)

    Begin with the treaty that directly names this band and its recorded tracts.

  2. Treaty with the Chippewa of Saginaw, etc., August 2, 1855 — selected transcription

    Compare the later instrument’s specifically defined parties remaining in Michigan.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

A directly named 1836 reading path

The 1836 text records cessions including land at the mouth of Black River of the St. Clair River. Article 4 promises replacement land west of the Mississippi or northwest of St. Anthony’s Falls. The text alone does not establish completed relocation.

Read the sources [2] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties; historical treaty text

02

Keep the 1855 parties specific

The later instrument addresses the portions remaining in Michigan alongside Saginaw parties. Read that scope before tracing later affiliations.

Read the sources [3] Clarke Historical Library, Central Michigan University; historical treaty text

03

Follow the shared community institution

Ziibiwing’s three-band statement supplies identity context. The photograph shows the Tribe’s shared cultural-history center; it does not depict a separate band government or establish descent.

Read the sources [1] Ziibiwing Center

Primary treaty / archive transcriptionOklahoma State University Libraries, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties; historical treaty textSource 2

Treaty with the Chippewa, May 9, 1836 (7 Stat. 503) ↗

Publication: Treaty dated May 9, 1836; proclamation May 25, 1836

The instrument specifically names Swan Creek and Black River bands, lists ceded tracts and promises proceeds and western land. Its recital of agreement is treaty language, not an independent account of consent or subsequent experience.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual transcription preamble, Articles 1–4, signatory and witness names, web lines 25–72 read. Linked original scan and underlying 1807 treaty not inspected; no claim of actual payment, completed relocation or present rights.

Review recorded: October 27, 2026

Primary treaty / archive transcriptionClarke Historical Library, Central Michigan University; historical treaty textSource 3

Treaty with the Chippewa of Saginaw, etc., August 2, 1855 — selected transcription ↗

Publication: Treaty dated August 2, 1855; web transcription undated

The 1855 text names its parties and sets out land-selection and payment provisions. It distinguishes Saginaw treaty parties from Swan Creek and Black River parties remaining in Michigan. Historical provisions are not current eligibility, boundaries or proof of fulfillment.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual Saginaw Chippewa and other Bands section, preamble and Articles 1–7, web lines 745–776 read. Other treaties on this long page, original signatures/scans, later implementation and current law not assessed.

Review recorded: October 27, 2026
